title: Building a REST API
subtitle: REST principles, CRUD routes, status codes, and input validation
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: HTTP is a generic protocol. Without conventions, every API would have different URL structures, response shapes, and error formats — making integration unpredictable.
whyItExists.solution: REST (Representational State Transfer) provides architectural conventions: use nouns for URLs (/users, /posts), HTTP methods for actions (GET=read, POST=create, PUT/PATCH=update, DELETE=delete), and standard status codes (200/201/400/404/500) for outcomes.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any HTTP API that multiple clients (frontend, mobile, third parties) will consume. REST is the default choice — familiar, cacheable, and tooling-rich.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For complex queries with many related resources, consider GraphQL. For real-time bidirectional communication, use WebSockets.

explainModes.beginner: A REST API is a web service with a consistent structure. Users are at /users. To get all users: GET /users. To get one: GET /users/1. To create: POST /users with a body. To update: PUT /users/1. To delete: DELETE /users/1. The HTTP method tells the server what action to take.
explainModes.simple: REST conventions: nouns in URLs (not /getUsers). Plural resource names (/users not /user). HTTP methods are the verbs. Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created (POST success), 204 No Content (DELETE success), 400 Bad Request (invalid input), 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable (validation), 500 Server Error. Collection: GET /users, POST /users. Item: GET /users/:id, PUT /users/:id, DELETE /users/:id.
explainModes.standard: CRUD mapping: Create → POST /resource (201 + new object), Read all → GET /resource (200 + array), Read one → GET /resource/:id (200 + object or 404), Update → PUT /resource/:id (full replace, 200) or PATCH (partial, 200), Delete → DELETE /resource/:id (200 or 204). Filtering/sorting: GET /users?role=admin&sort=name (query params). Pagination: GET /users?page=2&limit=10. Nested resources: GET /users/:id/posts. Response envelope: { data: [...], meta: { total, page } } for collections.
explainModes.technical: Idempotency: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent (calling twice has same effect). POST is not. PATCH is not necessarily. This distinction matters for retries. HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses include links to related actions — mostly theoretical for internal APIs. Content negotiation: Accept header. Versioning: /api/v1/users, or Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json header. ETag / If-None-Match: conditional requests for efficient caching.
explainModes.deepDive: OpenAPI spec (formerly Swagger): a YAML/JSON format that describes REST APIs. Tools generate client SDKs, server stubs, and interactive docs (Swagger UI) from a spec. swagger-jsdoc reads JSDoc comments; swagger-ui-express serves the UI. JSON:API specification: a stricter REST standard with a specific response shape — used for APIs with complex relationships. Hypermedia controls (HAL, JSON-LD): self-documenting APIs — each response includes links to related resources. Used in public APIs (GitHub REST API uses _links). Rate limiting: express-rate-limit middleware — limit requests per IP per window.

questions.question: A client creates a resource with POST /articles. What status code and response body should the server return?
options: 201 Created with the created resource (including its new id)
200 OK with a success message string
questions.explanation: 201 Created is the correct status for a successful POST that creates a resource. The response body should include the created object — especially its newly assigned id — so the client knows what was created without making a second request. 200 OK is for successful reads (GET). 204 No Content is for successful operations with no response body, like DELETE.

faq.q: When should I use PUT vs PATCH?
faq.a: PUT is a full replacement: the client sends the entire resource and the server replaces it. PATCH is a partial update: the client sends only the fields to change. In practice: use PUT when the client always sends the complete representation; use PATCH for partial edits (like toggling done: true on a todo). PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent (depends on implementation), but PUT always is.
